keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Aeolian (Natural Minor) with Harmonic Minor inflections

mainProgression.description: The verse is built on a simple but powerful two-chord alternation between Em and B7, with the dominant seventh chord borrowed from E harmonic minor creating dark, exotic tension

sectionProgressions.description: Hypnotic two-chord vamp creating the driving, urgent feel of the verses
Expanded progression adding harmonic movement with D and A chords before resolving back to B7
Same verse progression supporting the sitar-like guitar melody during instrumental sections

harmonicFunction: Em (i) - Tonic minor chord establishing the dark, urgent mood
B7 (V7) - Dominant seventh chord from E harmonic minor, creating strong pull back to Em
D (VII) - Subtonic adding harmonic variety in the chorus sections
A (IV) - Subdominant providing movement before the V7 resolution
The i-V7 vamp is the harmonic engine of the song, creating relentless drive
The raised 7th (D#) in B7 gives the song its exotic, quasi-Eastern flavor

techniques.name: Fast Minor Key Strumming
techniques.description: Driving eighth-note strumming pattern at 162 BPM alternating between Em and B7, requiring right-hand stamina and precise chord transitions at speed

notes: Em: 0-2-2-0-0-0 (Open Em chord)
B7: X-2-1-2-0-2 (Open B7 chord)
Continuous eighth-note strumming pattern (down-up-down-up) at 162 BPM
The tempo is very fast - consistent down-up strumming is essential
Slight dynamic accents on beats 1 and 3 drive the pulse
sequence: Establish the Em chord shape on the fretboard
Begin driving eighth-note down-up strumming pattern
Transition to B7 on the chord change - keep strumming through
Return to Em and maintain the relentless driving rhythm
tips: Keep the strumming arm loose and relaxed to maintain speed
Practice the Em to B7 change in isolation before adding the strumming pattern
Use a lighter pick gauge (0.60-0.73mm) for faster strumming comfort
Focus on the groove and feel rather than hitting every string perfectly
details.progression: Em - B7 - Em - B7 (driving 8th note rhythm)

techniques.name: Sitar-Emulating Guitar Melody
techniques.description: The distinctive single-note guitar line that mimics the sitar melody heard on the original recording, using hammer-ons and the E harmonic minor scale for its exotic character

notes: Based on E harmonic minor scale, emphasizing the D# (raised 7th) for exotic flavor
Single-note melody played on the higher strings (B and high E)
Uses hammer-ons and pull-offs for smooth, flowing articulation
Keith Richards originally played this line to emulate Brian Jones' sitar part
sequence: Position fingers on the high E and B strings around the open position and 2nd-4th frets
Pick the melody cleanly with precise single-note articulation
Use hammer-ons for the ascending notes within the phrase
Emphasize the D# note (4th fret B string) for the harmonic minor character
tips: Learn the E harmonic minor scale thoroughly before tackling this melody
Listen carefully to the original recording to match the phrasing and timing
Keep the tone clean or with very light overdrive for clarity
Practice at half speed to nail the exact note sequence before building tempo

techniques.name: Dynamic Chord Transitions
techniques.description: The expanded chord vocabulary in the chorus sections, moving through Em-D-A-B7 with smooth transitions and dynamic variation from the two-chord verse

notes: D: X-X-0-2-3-2 (Open D major chord)
A: X-0-2-2-2-0 (Open A major chord)
Smooth transitions between all four chords without breaking the strumming rhythm
Dynamic increase during the chorus for energy contrast with verses
sequence: Start on Em with the established driving strumming pattern
Move to D major chord with smooth finger repositioning
Shift to A major, keeping the strumming consistent
Resolve to B7 with the characteristic dominant tension
tips: Practice the D to A transition in isolation - it requires a full hand shape change
Anticipate each chord change by starting the finger movement slightly early
Maintain the driving eighth-note strumming through all changes
The dynamic increase into the chorus should feel natural, not forced

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: The song opens with the iconic sitar melody (originally played on an actual sitar by Brian Jones, now often covered on guitar) over the Em-B7 vamp, setting the dark, exotic tone
notes: The original features sitar, but guitar can emulate the melody line
Driving rhythm guitar enters almost immediately underneath
Establishes the driving tempo of 162 BPM from the start
The harmonic minor character is established through the melody and B7 chord

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The verse features relentless driving eighth-note strumming alternating Em and B7, creating the urgent, almost frantic energy that defines the song
notes: Continuous driving eighth-note strumming throughout
Two-chord vamp creates hypnotic, relentless energy
Dynamic level stays consistent to maintain the urgent mood
Guitar supports the vocal melody with rhythmic precision

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: The chorus expands the harmonic palette with a four-chord progression, adding D and A before resolving to B7 for a fuller, more dynamic sound
notes: Four-chord progression adds harmonic movement and variety
Dynamic increase from the verse level for chorus energy
Strumming pattern remains consistent through the chord changes
B7 resolution creates strong pull back to Em for the next section

sections.name: Instrumental Break
sections.description: Returns to the sitar/guitar melody over the Em-B7 vamp, with the full band maintaining the driving rhythm underneath
notes: Guitar melody takes the spotlight over the rhythm section
Same harmonic minor melody as the intro with possible variations
Rhythm guitar maintains the driving eighth-note strumming
Energy level stays high through the instrumental section

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: The song drives to its conclusion with the full band at maximum intensity, repeating the verse vamp as the energy builds to a final decisive ending
notes: Maximum intensity strumming with full dynamics
The urgency increases through the final repetitions
Clean ending rather than fade-out on the original recording
Maintain tempo precision through the final bars

guitar.recommended: Gibson Hummingbird acoustic or Fender Telecaster
alternatives: Any quality acoustic guitar for rhythm
Gibson ES-335 for the combined acoustic/electric tone
guitar.pickup: Single coils for the bright, cutting tone; acoustic with piezo for the rhythm part

effects.distortion: None to very light overdrive - the tone should be clean and cutting
effects.reverb: Light spring reverb for a touch of ambience
effects.other: No effects needed - the raw, driving sound is key to the song's energy

beginner.title: Getting Started with Paint It Black
steps: Learn the open Em and B7 chord shapes
Practice basic strumming patterns at slow tempo (80-100 BPM)
Work on transitioning cleanly between Em and B7
Learn the open D and A chord shapes for the chorus

intermediate.title: Building Speed and Adding the Melody
steps: Increase strumming speed gradually from 100 to 140 BPM
Learn the E harmonic minor scale for the melody line
Practice the sitar-emulating guitar melody at slow tempo
Work on the full song structure including verse and chorus transitions

advanced.title: Full Speed Performance and Expression
steps: Play the complete rhythm part at the original 162 BPM
Combine the melody and rhythm elements together
Develop stamina for the continuous driving strumming
Match the dynamics and energy shifts of the original recording

commonMistakes: Tensing up the strumming arm at the fast 162 BPM tempo, leading to fatigue
Sloppy B7 chord shape causing buzzing or muted strings
Losing the driving eighth-note rhythm during chord changes
Playing the melody line without the harmonic minor D# note, losing the exotic flavor
Not differentiating dynamics between verse and chorus sections
practiceRoutine: Warm up with Em to B7 chord changes at 80 BPM for 5 minutes
Practice driving eighth-note strumming on Em only, building to 130+ BPM
Add the B7 chord change while maintaining strumming pattern at 120 BPM
Work on the melody line separately using E harmonic minor at slow tempo
Play along with the original recording once comfortable at 150+ BPM
focusAreas: Right-hand strumming stamina and relaxation at high tempo
Clean Em to B7 transitions without breaking the strumming rhythm
Accurate E harmonic minor melody line with proper emphasis on D#
Dynamic contrast between verse (two-chord) and chorus (four-chord) sections
Maintaining absolutely steady tempo through the entire 3:22 duration
metronomeWork: Start strumming exercises at 80 BPM with eighth-note down-up pattern
Increase by 10 BPM per session while maintaining clean chord shapes
At 120 BPM, add the full Em-B7 chord change to the pattern
Practice the chorus chord changes (Em-D-A-B7) at 100 BPM before building speed
Target tempo is 162 BPM - prioritize consistent timing over speed
